post.title: MacParakeet: Fast, Local Voice on Apple Silicon
post.description: A builder's review of MacParakeet: NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT on Apple's Neural Engine for system-wide dictation, file and YouTube transcription, and meetings.
post.excerpt: I have a rule for voice tools: my audio does not leave my machine. MacParakeet, an open-source Mac app by Daniel Moon, runs NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT on the Apple Neural Engine for dictation, transcription, and meeting recording. Here is how it works, how to install it, and where it falls short.
post.content:
I have a rule for voice tools: my audio does not leave my machine. Dictation hears everything: half-formed ideas, client names, late-night thinking out loud. Routing that through someone's server for a monthly fee never sat right with me.

So when I found MacParakeet, an open-source voice app for Mac by Daniel Moon (moona3k on GitHub), I forked it the same week. Up front: this is his project, not mine. My fork at aryateja2106/macparakeet has zero commits of my own. This is a builder's review.

The README's tagline riffs on the Rifleman's Creed: "There are many voice transcription/dictation apps, but this one is mine." That line is the whole pitch. Open-source, local, and yours.

## The problem: rent a server or configure a model

The project's vision doc (spec/00-vision.md) names two failure modes of existing voice tools, and draws them as an ASCII diagram.

Cloud dictation apps like WisprFlow and Otter: Voice -> Server -> Wait -> Text -> "$12-15/mo forever". Your audio leaves the machine, you wait on a round trip, and you pay rent.

Local-but-complex apps like MacWhisper and Superwhisper: private, but you configure and select models yourself, and they cost "$30-$250".

MacParakeet's stated north star: "The fastest, most private voice app for Mac. Fully local speech when you want it. No required cloud subscription for core speech." The diagram's third row is just: Voice -> Text. Done.

All speech recognition runs on-device. No cloud STT path, no accounts, no login. Audio never leaves the Mac. The AI features (summaries, transcript chat, Transforms) are opt-in, and even those can stay local via Ollama or LM Studio. Today it is free and fully unlocked under GPL-3.0.

## What it does

Three jobs, one app:

- System-wide dictation: a hotkey in any app (default Fn, rebindable to F13/F19, End, or modifier chords), push-to-talk or hands-free, text pasted at your cursor.
- File, folder, and URL transcription: drag in files or a folder, or paste any link yt-dlp supports (YouTube, X, Vimeo, TikTok, Instagram). Apple Podcasts links resolve through the iTunes lookup API, no scraping.
- Meeting recording: system audio plus microphone, or either alone, with live local transcript preview, in-call notes, and audio retention controls (keep, auto-delete after N days, delete immediately). Calendar reminders and opt-in auto-start use local macOS EventKit, no Google or Microsoft sign-ins.

Exports cover seven formats: TXT, Markdown, SRT, VTT, DOCX, PDF, and JSON, with word-level timestamps and speaker labels when the engine provides timings.

## Install it

The app ships as a notarized DMG in the official homebrew/cask repo, no tap needed. I verified the cask exists by running `brew info --cask macparakeet`: version 0.6.24, arm64 only, macOS 14 or newer.

```bash
brew install --cask macparakeet
```

The standalone CLI comes from the author's tap, pulls in Homebrew-managed ffmpeg and yt-dlp, and shares the app's local database and model cache.

```bash
brew install moona3k/tap/macparakeet-cli
```

The repo also documents a build-from-source path. Its dev script builds, signs a .app bundle so macOS grants microphone and accessibility permissions, and launches it. I read the script but have not run this build myself.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/moona3k/macparakeet.git
cd macparakeet
swift test
scripts/dev/run_app.sh
```

One caveat: first launch downloads about 465 MB of Parakeet CoreML weights plus about 130 MB of speaker-detection assets. Local, yes. Zero-download out of the box, no.

## How it works

1.  **NVIDIA's model on Apple's NPU**: The default engine is Parakeet TDT 0.6B, an NVIDIA ASR model, executed on the Apple Neural Engine through the FluidAudio CoreML runtime. That cross-vendor detail is my favorite thing in the codebase. Input is 16kHz mono Float32; FluidAudio handles resampling and decoding. Upstream's README claims roughly 155x realtime, about 60 minutes of audio in about 23 seconds. I have not benchmarked it myself, so treat those as the author's numbers.

2.  **Three Parakeet builds, user-selectable**: Multilingual v3 is the default, covering English plus 24 European languages with word-level timestamps and per-word confidence. English-only v2 is slightly faster and cannot mis-detect language. Parakeet Unified streams natively with built-in punctuation and capitalization but gives up word timings. Optional engines slot into the same control plane: Nemotron (Beta, streaming, multilingual), WhisperKit for broad language coverage, Cohere Transcribe for batch accuracy. All on-device.

3.  **An architecture that protects dictation latency**: A SwiftUI layer sits over MacParakeetCore, a library with no UI dependencies. Three services (dictation, transcription, meeting recording) feed an AudioProcessor into an STT scheduler that reserves a dedicated inference slot for dictation and shares a second slot between meeting and file jobs, so a long file transcription cannot block a quick dictation. Persistence is a single SQLite file via GRDB. The live dictation preview never feeds the paste; final text comes from the stop-time transcription path, with a LiveTranscriptStabilizer keeping shown words monotonic.

4.  **Text cleanup is deliberately not AI**: A deterministic pipeline, under 1ms per the README, strips fillers, applies custom word replacements, expands snippet trigger phrases longest-first, and handles a spoken "Voice Return" trigger that simulates a Return keypress. Both raw and cleaned transcripts are stored. No LLM in the hot path.

5.  **Permission-minimized meeting capture**: Meetings combine ScreenCaptureKit for system audio with AVAudioEngine for the microphone. Microphone-only mode skips the macOS Screen Recording permission entirely, a design choice I wish more apps made.

6.  **One systems-level gem**: Package.swift includes a dedicated Objective-C shim target whose only job is catching NSExceptions from AppKit, AVFoundation, and Core Audio, which Swift's do/try/catch cannot catch. If you write Swift against C-era Apple frameworks, steal that pattern.

## The CLI is built for agents

This is where MacParakeet lines up with how I work as an Agentic Engineer. The integrations README literally opens with "If you are a coding agent working in this repo..." Every read-only CLI command emits JSON with schemas pinned to the major CLI version, and failures carry a stable errorType so agents can branch deterministically.

One-off transcription for shell pipelines, without saving to history:

```bash
macparakeet-cli transcribe /path/to/audio.mp3 --format transcript --no-history
```

Freetext podcast search: it queries the iTunes directory, parses the show's RSS feed, picks the episode, then downloads and transcribes locally.

```bash
macparakeet-cli transcribe --podcast "Lex Fridman episode 400"
```

Model management, shared between the app and the CLI:

```bash
macparakeet-cli models list
macparakeet-cli models download nemotron-multilingual-1120ms
macparakeet-cli models select parakeet-v3
```

Switching the Parakeet build through the same preference suite the GUI reads:

```bash
macparakeet-cli config set parakeet-model v2
```

And a machine-readable health check:

```bash
macparakeet-cli health --json
```

The repo also ships AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and a spec/ directory with ADRs, including one on the AI coding method used to build it. This codebase expects coding agents to work on it.

## Honest limitations

- Not my project. Worth repeating: aryateja2106/macparakeet is a fork of moona3k/macparakeet, 0 commits ahead and 120 behind as of this writing. Daniel Moon is the author, and sponsorship links go to him.
- Apple Silicon only (M1-M4), macOS 14.2 or newer. No Intel Macs.
- Parakeet is best for English plus 24 European languages. Other languages need the optional Nemotron, WhisperKit, or Cohere engines, each with a separate model download (Nemotron multilingual is about 1.5 GB).
- Cohere Transcribe is batch-only: no live preview, no word timestamps, no speaker labels. Nemotron is Beta pending real-world benchmarking.
- Telemetry is opt-out, on by default, even for source builds. It is non-identifying and self-hosted, and the README links straight to TelemetryService.swift with a "verify it yourself" pointer. I like the receipts, but know the default.
- Only core speech recognition is fully local. AI features, Sparkle update checks, yt-dlp downloads, and iTunes lookups all use the network.
- My verification stopped at reading the repo and running `brew info --cask macparakeet`. I did not build the app, run the CLI, or measure performance. The word error rates upstream cites (~2.5% for v3, ~2.1% for v2) are the author's claims.

## What's next

Three things. First, the daily-driver test: dictation as my default input for a week, and the CLI wired into my agent workflows so an agent can transcribe a podcast episode and summarize it with a local model. Second, sync my fork; 120 commits behind defeats the point of having one. Third, send anything worth fixing upstream: a GPL-3.0 codebase with an agent-ready CLI is one I want to contribute to, not just review.

If you are on Apple Silicon and still paying monthly rent to dictate into your own computer, try this instead.
